text: Janice Burgess (March 1, 1952 – March 2, 2024) was an American television executive, screenwriter, and producer for Nickelodeon. She created the Nick Jr. series The Backyardigans and served as a writer and story editor for Nickelodeon's revival of Winx Club, both of which were produced at the Nickelodeon Animation Studio. Burgess joined Nickelodeon in 1995 as executive-in-charge of production. Born in Pittsburgh, Pennsylvania, she grew up in the Squirrel Hill neighborhood and attended the Ellis School. She frequently played in her backyard, which later inspired The Backyardigans, describing it as a "wonderful, happy, safe place" where "you could have these great adventures just romping around. From there, you could go anywhere or do anything." She loved musicals, and her mother frequently played a wide array of music. Planning to become an art historian, she graduated from Brandeis University in 1974 with a bachelor's degree in art history. According to an interview with Investor's Business Daily, Burgess did not enjoy traveling "in art circles with collectors and high society," so she sought a different career after college and volunteered at public television station WQED, where she managed craft services. In the early 1990s, she held positions at the Children's Television Workshop, including as an assistant travel coordinator for 3-2-1 Contact and project manager for Ghostwriter, where she coordinated tie-in magazine and teacher materials with the show's content. She was notified of a job opening at Nickelodeon and joked she interviewed "about 11,000 times." She was hired as executive in charge of production for Nick Jr., overseeing the development of Blue's Clues and Little Bill, and later became vice president of Nickelodeon's Nick Jr. division. While working as an executive, she attended scripting and concept development meetings and helped creative teams with characters and storylines. She was given a creative opportunity by senior vice president Brown Johnson, who asked her to develop a new Nick Jr. show. Burgess produced a pilot episode called "Me and My Friends" at Nickelodeon Studios Florida in 1998, a live-action, full-body puppet show featuring music and dance, which was not picked up for a full series. Several months later, Brown Johnson asked her to retool the concept, as he liked the characters and music and believed the show would work better in animation. Using the characters from "Me and My Friends," she wrote a second pilot produced at Nickelodeon's New York studio in 2002, which was renamed The Backyardigans and greenlit for a 20-episode season. Reflecting on the shift, Burgess said, "Sometimes your first attempt is just not all that great. In this case, my second attempt was much better." The Backyardigans premiered on Nickelodeon on October 11, 2004. Burgess served as executive producer for the show throughout its four-season run. In 2006, she described her work positively: "making The Backyardigans has become sort of like an adventure that I go on with my friends. Of course, we get paid, but we do get to be carefree in our work, enjoy each other, hang around a lot, travel a little bit, and make up stuff." She drew inspiration from action films, such as Die Hard and Terminator 2, when writing episodes, aiming to adapt high-stakes stories for young children in a safe, non-scary, and non-imitatable way. The series received eight Daytime Emmy Award nominations, and Burgess won the 2008 Emmy for Outstanding Special Class Animated Program. After The Backyardigans concluded in 2010 with its fourth and final season, much of the staff, including Burgess, regrouped to work on Nickelodeon's Winx Club, where she served as a writer, story editor, and creative consultant. Burgess died in hospice care in Manhattan on March 2, 2024, the day after her 72nd birthday. She was diagnosed with breast cancer in 2018, six years before her death.
